claims.text: Adding approximately 3–5 at.% zirconium to a phosphorus-containing compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability relative to the zirconium-free baseline.
Adding approximately 3–5 at.% zirconium will increase the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state relative to the zirconium-free baseline.
The baseline phosphorus-containing alloy has a known tendency to form a metastable amorphous phase under rapid solidification.
The beneficial effect should occur when the modified and baseline alloys are processed under comparable cooling conditions.
The beneficial effect is limited to a narrow zirconium concentration window around 3–5 at.%.
Zirconium additions above the proposed concentration range may diminish the benefits.
Thermal histories significantly different from that of the baseline may prevent the proposed benefits.
The zirconium addition increases atomic-size mismatch.
The zirconium addition increases chemical disorder.
Increased atomic-size mismatch and chemical disorder disrupt crystalline nucleation sites.
The zirconium-induced structural changes retard atomic mobility.
Greater compositional complexity and atomic-size mismatch promote topological frustration.
Topological frustration suppresses crystalline-phase nucleation during cooling.
Topological frustration suppresses crystalline-phase growth during cooling.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a wider supercooled-liquid region than the baseline.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline.
The zirconium-modified alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for amorphous-phase formation than the baseline.
